name: Parachute Drop Challenge
overview: Students design, build, and test a parachute for a small toy to reduce its landing speed and impact force. Teams iterate their designs under time and material constraints, aiming to achieve the slowest and safest landing within a target area.
equipment: Mobile phone with STEMM Lab app

instruction.text: Drop the toy without a parachute and record the fall (baseline test).
Build a parachute using provided materials.
Drop the toy from the same height and record the fall.
Review speed and landing accuracy results in the app.
Redesign and test up to three prototypes within 20 minutes.
Upload videos, results, and team reflections.

label: Toy attached to parachute
Drop height marked
Target landing zone shown on floor

question: Predict which parachute design was the best.
Sketch each of the design
Recode the times of the design
Were you correct in timings?
What design was the easiest to make?

discussion.title: Parachutes and Forces
discussion.description: Gravity pulls objects downward, causing them to speed up as they fall. A parachute increases air resistance (also called drag). Drag acts upward, opposing the motion and slowing the fall. A slower fall reduces the force when the toy hits the ground, making the landing safer. Engineers improve parachute designs through repeated testing and redesign.

calculations.title: Measure the Drop Height
calculations.description: Measure the height of the table or drop surface (distance fallen).

calculations.title: Measure the Time
description: Drop the toy (do not throw it).
Record the time taken to first hit the ground using a phone or video.

calculations.title: Calculate Final Velocity
description: Since the toy is dropped, the initial velocity is 0 m/s.

calculations.title: Calculate Net Force
description: Net Force = 0.20 kg x 4 m/s² = 0.8 N

calculations.title: Calculate Drag Force
description: Weight = mass × g = 0.20 kg x 9.8 m/s² = 1.96 N
Drag Force = Weight - Net force = 1.96 N - 0.8 N = 1.16 N

gForce.description: G-force describes how quickly the object slows down when it hits the ground. It is measured in multiples of g = 9.8 m/s².
slowMotionInstruction: Identify the moment the toy first hits the ground
Measure the time taken for the toy to stop moving (contact time)

cases.title: Object Does Not Bounce
cases.description: Object goes from impact speed downward to 0 m/s.

cases.title: Object Bounces
cases.description: Object goes from impact speed downward to updward velocity at separation (𝑣Up).

additionalCalculation.title: Finding 𝑣Up if rebound height is unknown
additionalCalculation.description: Measure time to maximum height after bounce (𝑡up) using slow-motion video.

example: Time to max height after bounce: 0.15 s → 𝑣Up = 9.8 × 0.15 ≈ 1.47 m/s
cases.observation: Bouncing increases g-force because the velocity change during contact is larger.

tips: Use a ruler in frame for scale
Identify first contact for contact time
Identify when object leaves surface for bounce calculation

injuryRisk.title: Typical G-Force Ranges and Injury Risk

ranges.example: Standing up quicly, elevators or amusement rides
Hard falls while running or minor car braking
Sports collisions, bicycle crashes or car crashes with seatbelts
ranges.effect: Serious injuries possible (broken bones or concussions

ranges.example: Servere car crashes or falls onto hard surface
Very sudden stops with no cushioning

injuryRisk.Important: Duration matters. A brief spike can be survivable, while sustained g-forces are more dangerous.
